outcome: Chen, Li & Zhong (arXiv:2609.08251, 8 Sep 2026) raise the lower bound for arbitrary isometric fillings to 14ζ(3)/π, beating the Briggs–Wells 1.36π bound. [Judged 2026-09-28; the researcher's original outcome follows.] The full conjecture remains open, but two preprints since the frozen revision have moved the quantitative lower bound on the area of arbitrary (not just disk- or genus-one) isometric fillings of a length-2π circle: Briggs & Wells (Feb 2026) proved a bound of 1.36π via a discrete graph-theoretic analogue, and Chen, Li & Zhong (Sep 2026) improved this to 14ζ(3)/π ≈ 5.357 (about 1.706π) using a Fourier-coefficient method, with a stronger bound for orientable fillings — both still well short of the conjectured 2π.
summary: The filling area conjecture (Gromov, 1983) — that the hemisphere minimizes area among orientable Riemannian surfaces isometrically filling a boundary circle of given length — remains fully open since the frozen revision. The Wikipedia article itself has not been updated past 2011-era citations and still presents it as open. Two arXiv preprints from 2026 make genuine progress by proving quantitative lower bounds applicable to *arbitrary* isometric fillings (not restricted to disks or genus-one surfaces, where the conjecture was already known): Briggs & Wells, 'A discrete view of Gromov's filling area conjecture' (arXiv:2602.17859, submitted 19 Feb 2026), translate the problem into a discrete graph-theoretic analogue using Menger's theorem to get the first quantitative lower bound (1.36π) covering all fillings, not requiring orientability. Chen, Li & Zhong, 'A Fourier approach to Gromov's filling area conjecture' (arXiv:2609.08251, submitted 8 Sep 2026), use odd Fourier coefficients of boundary-distance functions plus a cubic resonant perturbation for the orientable case to push the universal lower bound to 14ζ(3)/π ≈ 5.357, with a stronger bound for orientable surfaces. Both results move the known lower bound closer to the conjectured 2π (≈6.283) but do not resolve the conjecture; neither has yet been digested by expert commentary (no Tao blog post, Quanta piece, or journal acceptance found), so both are correctly `claimed`-tier work but the record as a whole is `progress` since the bound moved without any single result being a full resolution — no case of the conjecture (e.g. a new topological class) was fully settled either. A related preprint, 'An Upper Bound for Discrete Isometric Filling of Cycles' (arXiv:2605.08909), explicitly notes its discrete construction 'cannot be used to settle Gromov's conjecture' — a related/variant result, not counted here. No AI system was mentioned in any of these papers, their abstracts, methods sections, or acknowledgements; all methods described (graph theory/Menger's theorem, Fourier analysis, cubic resonant perturbation) are classical continuous/discrete mathematics with no computational or machine-learning component disclosed. I found no news coverage, lab announcement, or AI system card referencing the filling area conjecture at all.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `claimed` rather than `progress`, since each individual preprint is itself an unresolved claim awaiting expert digestion. I chose `progress` because the rules describe `progress` as covering 'a bound moved,' which is the more specific and applicable code here, and because the conjecture proper is unaffected — both papers are explicitly about moving a quantitative bound on filling area, not proposing a proof of the conjecture itself.
what_would_settle_it: Expert digestion (e.g., a referee report, journal acceptance, or a well-known geometer's blog commentary) confirming the Briggs-Wells or Chen-Li-Zhong bounds, or — more decisively — a full proof (or disproof) of the conjecture in its stated generality (hemisphere as the area minimizer among all shortcut-free fillings, not just disk or genus-one cases).
